analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace anti-harassment and discrimination laws, bans forced arbitration of those claims, and gradually ends the lower tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late July 2024, the bill was sent to five House committees, received no hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025; all 38 House supporters were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers to adopt and enforce anti-harassment policies and training, make it easier for workers to sue over harassment and discrimination, extend those protections to independent contractors and interns, and ban forced arbitration and certain nondisclosure agreements in discrimination cases. It also would gradually raise the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped employees until it equals the full federal minimum wage, and fund legal help for low-income workers with discrimination claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination on the job, especially tipped workers (whose base cash wage would rise from $2.13 an hour to the full federal minimum), LGBTQ workers (whose protection would be written into statute), gig and contract workers, interns, and low-income workers who would get grant-funded legal help. All workers at employers with as few as one employee would gain coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every employer with 15 or more employees to maintain, post, and annually distribute a comprehensive nondiscrimination policy, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for repeated or willful violations), and directs the EEOC to set rules requiring anti-harassment training. [S2]

Writes into statute that harassment is unlawful discrimination, lets a single incident count, and requires courts to weigh harassing conduct as a whole rather than dismissing it as not 'severe or pervasive' enough. [S2]

Removes the caps on compensatory and punitive damages in discrimination cases, extends the time workers have to file claims, and makes employers with as few as one employee covered by civil rights employment law (currently 15). [S2]
Bans mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims and limits nondisclosure agreements, and extends protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees. [S2]

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage: employers would pay tipped workers a cash wage starting at $3.60 an hour, rising by up to $1.50 a year until it equals the full federal minimum, after which tipped employees are paid the standard minimum wage and keep their tips. [S2]

Creates grants for civil legal help for low-income workers facing employment discrimination and for a state advocacy system, and orders a first-ever national survey of how often workplace harassment occurs. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: compliance spending on policies and training, fines for noncompliance, higher wages for tipped employees as the tip credit phases out, larger lawsuit exposure from uncapped damages and easier legal standards, and the loss of mandatory arbitration and broad nondisclosure agreements as shields. Restaurant and hospitality operators using the $2.13 tipped wage would see the largest direct payroll increase.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small operators: every covered employer must build policies, run interactive training, and post materials, and the bill lowers the coverage threshold to employers with just one employee, sweeping in tiny businesses. [S2]

The litigation changes cut in one direction only: no damages caps, longer filing windows, a motivating-factor standard, and a rule that a single incident can create liability would raise legal exposure and settlement costs for employers of every size, and some of that cost gets passed to workers through reduced hiring or hours. [S2]

Ending the tip credit raises full-service restaurant labor costs sharply during the phase-in; opponents of tipped-wage elimination have long argued it accelerates closures and cut hours in the industry. [S2]
The bill removes the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense in Title VII cases, a provision critics view as an unwarranted override of religious-liberty protections. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is substantial: stronger, cheaper-to-use legal remedies against harassment and discrimination, coverage for gig workers and tiny employers, and a full minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs are real but diffuse: compliance and legal exposure for employers, with the heaviest burden on restaurants and small businesses, and some risk of reduced hours or hiring. The bill is broad and ambitious rather than narrowly targeted, which is part of why it drew no Republican support.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with five House committees after its July 2024 introduction, never got a hearing or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on July 30, 2024, joined by 19 original cosponsors. [S2]
The bill was referred to five committees at once: Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Accountability, and Veterans' Affairs. [S4]
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever taken; the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025. [S4]
It finished with 37 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support. [S3]
With divided government and a crowded end-of-session calendar, bills introduced this late with single-party sponsorship and five-committee referrals almost never move. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the compliance costs, higher tipped wages, and expanded lawsuit exposure are better off, since the bill never advanced; workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 19 original cosponsors. [S2]

for.name: 37 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did. [S3]

against.name: House committee chairs (five committees)
against.role: Chairs of Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Accountability, and Veterans' Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, for the six months remaining in the Congress. [S4]

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor agenda in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote. [S4]

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, in a House controlled by Republicans, and no Republican committee ever acted on it. [S3]

industries.industry: Restaurants and hospitality (employers using the tipped minimum wage)
industries.note: The bill phases out the $2.13 tip credit, requiring these employers to pay tipped staff up to the full federal minimum wage while tips stay with workers. Their cost is tipped workers' raise. [S2]
Mandatory policies, training, fines, uncapped damages, longer filing windows, and a single-incident liability standard raise both compliance costs and lawsuit exposure. [S2]

industries.industry: Employers using mandatory arbitration and broad NDAs (and the arbitration industry)
industries.note: The bill bans forced arbitration of discrimination claims and limits nondisclosure agreements, removing the private, off-the-record path that keeps many claims out of court. [S2]

industries.industry: Staffing platforms and businesses built on independent contractors
industries.note: Contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees would gain full anti-harassment and anti-discrimination protections they currently lack. [S2]
